status: UNVERIFIED design; no secret value exists in this repository
rules: A value lives in exactly one store of record. The repository, images, compose files, Terraform code and logs hold names only.

Runtime secrets reach a host ONLY through /usr/local/sbin/df-secrets-install (root-owned, installed by cloud-init, the single command the deploy user may sudo) as /run/dungeonflux/secrets/<consumer>/<file>, root:dfs-<consumer> 0440, in a 0750 directory of that group. /run is tmpfs: Droplet backups and snapshots never contain a secret. A reboot empties it on purpose; the deploy script pushes again.

ONE group per consumer. A service runs with its consumer's gid as primary group and mounts only its own DIRECTORY (never single files, so a rotation by rename does not break the mount). A campaign runtime's group has no identity, payment, provider, storage, journal or other-role database secret (checked by deploy/scripts/secrets-audit.sh manifest).
Provider credentials exist only in the egress dispatcher (decision 18). Runtimes reach PostgreSQL, the dispatcher, the media gateway (mTLS) and the telemetry ingestor only (decision 23).

No login account is in the docker group: containers are started only by root through df-deploy (validated arguments, cosign verification in round 2). One uid per service; runtime slots get 20000 + slot.
The game binary reads no environment variables: configuration is one TOML file, secrets are *_file paths into /run/secrets.
Credentials are separate by purpose (plan 12.7): deployment, one database role per service, payments, storage per bucket domain, backup writer, recovery journal, providers.
Production and staging never share a value or a store entry. Staging payment, identity and email keys are test-mode or sandbox only; secrets-push.sh refuses a live-looking value in staging.

Application database passwords are created by deploy/db/create-roles.sh from operator-generated files and never pass through Terraform. Terraform state does hold the cluster administrator credential, so the state bucket is a secret store.

RESIDUAL (ruling f): managed PostgreSQL has no pg_hba control and its trusted source is the whole Droplet, so database role separation in production rests on the secrecy of each role's password (one secrets directory and group per service) and on the grants, not on a source-address pin. Staging pins roles to source addresses where its topology allows (deploy/compose/postgres-init/pg_hba.conf); production cannot.
Company provider spend caps stay OFF (standing rule); a compromised key is handled by rotation, not by a cap.

launch_gates.rule: BUILT in round 2 (df-deploy refresh-keys and df-keys-apply) but never run: it closes only when it has been exercised on the STAGING environment (add a key, remove a key, remove the CI key and confirm the lockout is recoverable only by console, tamper with the signature and confirm refusal). The FIRST PRODUCTION terraform apply must not happen before then. SSH keys are root-owned files written once by first-boot cloud-init and Terraform changes never reach a running host, so without that tool a stolen or departed person's key can be revoked on a running host only through the DigitalOcean console or by replacing the host. Staging may be applied without it; production may not.

BUILT in round 2 (df-deploy release verifies the release image and every image by digest against the pinned certificate identity and OIDC issuer) but never run, and the CI job that builds, signs and publishes the release and key-set images is round 3. Until a signed release has been verified and a tampered one refused on staging, the CI deploy key is root-equivalent in effect; production must not take real traffic or money before that.

recurring_operations.rule: Replace the bastion MONTHLY: it has no outbound 80/443 (unless package_mirror_cidrs is set) and installs nothing at first boot, so it is patched only by replacement. It holds no state or secret. Command (from the environment root): terraform apply -replace='module.bastion[0].module.droplet.digitalocean_droplet.this[0]'.
recurring_operations.dependency: The CI key on the bastion is restricted by sshd permitopen to the LITERAL private addresses of the application and worker hosts, written once at the bastion's first boot. When an application or worker host is replaced its address changes and CI deploys fail until the bastion is replaced too (same command, after the host replacement). Replace the bastion in the same change as any host replacement.

delivery_kinds.host: pushed to /run/dungeonflux/secrets/<consumer>/ on every host whose role is in 'hosts' (the app host plays the worker role while worker_droplet_count is 0: use --roles app,worker)
delivery_kinds.ci-only: exists only as a protected GitHub environment secret or an OIDC-issued short-lived credential; never on a host
delivery_kinds.operator-only: held by named humans in the password manager; never on a production host
delivery_kinds.terraform-input: supplied to terraform as environment variables from the protected CI environment; never in tfvars files
delivery_kinds.runner-issued: written by the trusted runner into a runtime's own directory at placement time; never pushed by an operator

staging_policy.note: Staging uses fakes and test-mode or sandbox credentials only (coordinator decision e).

procedures.signing-key-epoch: Create the new key; push it as the current file and keep the old one as <file>.previous for the verification overlap (default 24h, never longer than the longest token lifetime); new tokens use the current key only; revoked tokens stop regardless of overlap; remove .previous after the overlap (a later push without it deletes it). Needs the key-set support named in the requests to B and O1.
procedures.database-password: Generate a new password file (deploy/scripts/gen-secret.sh), run deploy/db/create-roles.sh from an operator machine to ALTER the role, push the new file, restart the canary then the rest, verify readiness, record. Plan a brief connection reset; prefer a low-traffic window. Application passwords never touch Terraform state.
procedures.storage-key: Create a new Spaces access key with the same per-bucket grants, push it, restart canary then the rest, verify media and export operations, then revoke the old key and confirm its last-use time is before the push.
procedures.provider-key: Create a new key at the provider, push it to the dispatcher, verify, then revoke the old key; inspect dispatch and audit records between the old key's last use and revocation for unexpected spend. Only the egress dispatcher ever holds a provider key.
procedures.webhook-secret: Roll the endpoint secret at the processor using its overlap feature; accept both the current and previous secret for the overlap window; drop the previous one afterwards. Replay the durable inbox afterwards.
procedures.age-recipient: Generate a new age key pair offline; add the new public key to the backup recipients (backups encrypt to both); keep the old private key until the last backup encrypted only to it has aged out (30 days default); then retire it.
procedures.ci-credential: Prefer OIDC federation or short-lived tokens. For a static token: create the replacement, update the GitHub environment secret, run a no-op deploy dry run, delete the old token.
procedures.tls-and-ssh: KEYS ARE ROOT-OWNED FILES (/etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d/<user>), written ONCE by first-boot cloud-init: a Terraform change reaches only NEW hosts, because the droplet resource ignores user_data changes. A key is added or REVOKED on an existing host by `df-deploy refresh-keys <digest of the signed key-set image>` (CI only; the image holds the CI key and one FIDO2 key per person, is verified against the pinned identity and issuer, and is applied by df-keys-apply). Built in round 2, NOT YET EXERCISED (launch gate refresh-keys). If a host cannot be reached, the DigitalOcean console is the fallback. The bastion is not covered (no registry access): replace it monthly. Do not rely on removing a key from Terraform to revoke it. This is a LAUNCH GATE (see launch_gates): production is not applied before the tool has been exercised on staging. Public certificates for the edge are issued and renewed automatically.
procedures.internal-pki: THREE intermediate CAs under an offline internal root (decision 33), each CA:TRUE with pathlen:0. The RUNTIME-SERVER issuer is online, held by the control plane alone, serverAuth only: it signs each placement's game-listener certificate (URI SAN urn:dungeonflux:placement-server:<id>); the control plane's edge module pins it for runtime upstreams and checks the id. The other two: The SERVICE issuer (key offline, operator-only) signs the fixed identities and the server certificates; the PLACEMENT issuer (key on the runner) signs only the per-placement runtime client certificates. Every receiver pins both issuer certificates and enforces: a placement identity only through the placement issuer, a fixed identity only through the service issuer. Service certificates are short-lived (30 days): issue replacements on an operator machine, push, restart canary then the rest. Runtime client certificates are issued per placement by the runner and never pushed. Placement issuer rotation: issue the new one, push to the receivers and the runner (both certificates trusted during the overlap), switch the runner, remove the old one.

secrets.name: placement_issuer_key
secrets.description: Private key of the PLACEMENT ISSUER: an intermediate CA, signed by the internal CA, that the runner uses to mint each runtime's short-lived client certificate (URI SAN urn:dungeonflux:placement:<id>). It can mint only placement identities BY CONVENTION, because X.509 name constraints do not apply to URN SANs: every receiving service (media gateway, dispatcher, ingestor) therefore accepts a placement identity only from a chain that passes through this issuer and refuses the fixed identities (urn:dungeonflux:dispatcher, urn:dungeonflux:control-plane) from any chain that does (request.md, O1). Runner only.
secrets.generated_by: operator (internal CA; TODO(O1): custody and the receiving-side chain check)
secrets.on_compromise: Replace the issuer certificate on every receiver, issue a new one, restart the runner; every running placement is re-placed. P1: an attacker with this key can speak as any campaign to the media gateway, the dispatcher and the ingestor until it is replaced.

secrets.name: placement_issuer_certificate
secrets.description: PUBLIC certificate of the placement issuer (the chain a runtime presents is leaf + this). The runner presents it; the control plane, the dispatcher and the ingestor PIN it: a urn:dungeonflux:placement:<id> identity is accepted only from a chain that passes through exactly this certificate. It is issued with basicConstraints CA:TRUE, pathlen:0, so it cannot issue another CA.
secrets.on_compromise: Public data.

secrets.name: release_environment
secrets.description: KEY=VALUE lines of the NON-SECRET values a release needs that Terraform cannot give the Droplet at first boot (the database cluster is created after the Droplets): DB_HOST (the managed cluster's private host), DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_SERVER_NAME (the name the cluster certificate carries), INSTANCE_ID, ENVIRONMENT, SPACES_ENDPOINT, SPACES_REGION, BUCKET_PREFIX. df-deploy release substitutes them for the @NAME@ tokens in the release's config files and refuses a missing or unsafe value. Read only by root.
secrets.generated_by: terraform output plus the operator (deploy/scripts/render-release-environment.sh prints the file from the outputs)
secrets.on_compromise: Public data.

secrets.name: service_issuer_certificate
secrets.description: PUBLIC certificate of the SERVICE issuer, the second intermediate CA (CA:TRUE, pathlen:0) under the internal root. It signs the fixed identities (urn:dungeonflux:control-plane, urn:dungeonflux:dispatcher, the ingestor and gateway server certificates). EVERY CLIENT that verifies a service server pins it too (the edge upstream and healthcheck, the control plane's and the dispatcher's telemetry and gateway clients, the runtimes), so a certificate from the placement intermediate is never accepted as a server. The control plane, the dispatcher and the ingestor PIN it: a fixed identity is accepted only from a chain through this certificate and NEVER from one through the placement issuer, so a compromised runner (which holds the placement issuer key) cannot speak as the dispatcher.
secrets.on_compromise: Re-issue the service issuer and every fixed-identity certificate; P1.

secrets.name: service_issuer_key
secrets.description: Private key of the SERVICE issuer. OPERATOR-ONLY and offline: it signs the 30-day service certificates on an operator machine and never reaches a host (the runner, which IS exposed to runtimes, holds only the placement issuer key).
secrets.on_compromise: Treat every service certificate as compromised: re-issue the issuer and every certificate; P1.

secrets.name: runtime_server_issuer_certificate
secrets.description: PUBLIC certificate of the RUNTIME-SERVER issuer, the third intermediate CA (serverAuth only, CA:TRUE, pathlen:0, DNS constraint permitting nothing) under the internal root (decision 33). The control plane's edge module PINS it for every runtime upstream and checks the URI SAN urn:dungeonflux:placement-server:<id> against the placement id of the directory row it routed to. The Caddy edge never connects to a runtime and does not hold it.
secrets.on_compromise: Re-issue the issuer; every running placement gets a new listener certificate.

secrets.name: runtime_server_issuer_key
secrets.description: Private key of the RUNTIME-SERVER issuer. The ONLINE intermediate: the control plane holds it and NO other consumer does, so that it can sign each placement's game-listener certificate (URI SAN urn:dungeonflux:placement-server:<id>) at placement time. It can only sign serverAuth certificates with no DNS name, so a compromise lets an attacker impersonate a runtime listener to the control plane for the lifetime of the key, not impersonate a service, a client or the dispatcher.
secrets.on_compromise: Treat every game-listener certificate as untrusted: re-issue the issuer, push to the control plane and the pins, restart canary then the rest; P1.

secrets.name: internal_tls_runtime_key
secrets.description: Per-placement private key of the runtime's single mTLS client certificate (URI SAN urn:dungeonflux:placement:<placement id>), used toward the media gateway, the dispatcher and the telemetry ingestor; each takes the placement id from the certificate, never from the request. Issued by the runner into the slot's own secrets directory as a 0400 file owned by the slot uid (20000 + slot), so one runtime cannot read another's; never pushed by an operator.
secrets.on_compromise: Stop the placement; the fence rejects its writes.

secrets.name: internal_tls_runtime_certificate

secrets.on_compromise: Stop the placement; the fence rejects its writes.

Issued by the runner into the slot's own secrets directory as a 0400 file owned by the slot uid (20000 + slot), so one runtime cannot read another's; never pushed by an operator.
secrets.on_compromise: Stop the placement; the fence rejects its writes.

secrets.name: game_listener_key

secrets.name: offsite_access_key_id
secrets.description: OPTIONAL second backup destination outside the production credentials' destructive authority (coordinator decision h): a credential for a second S3-compatible target in another account or provider that CANNOT delete or overwrite what it wrote: either a credential that is write-only at that provider, or any credential on a bucket under OBJECT LOCK (compliance-mode retention it cannot shorten). A Spaces-style key alone is NOT enough. The endpoint must be https. The provider is deliberately UNSET; the interface is deploy/config/backup.env.example. The owner chooses it and decides how the journal head watermark is held.
secrets.on_compromise: Revoke; verify off-site copies; P1.

secrets.name: backup_age_recipient

secrets.on_compromise: A leaked recipient is harmless; a leaked private key means every backup encrypted to it is exposed: rotate the pair and re-encrypt retained backups.

secrets.name: registry_pull_token
secrets.description: Read-only token for pulling private images by digest (df-deploy logs in before it verifies or pulls; the user name is registry_user in /etc/dungeonflux/release-source). Unneeded if images are public; then do not push it. NEVER written to a Droplet disk: the deploy script logs in with DOCKER_CONFIG=/run/dungeonflux/docker (tmpfs) and passes the token on stdin, so ~/.docker/config.json never exists and Droplet backups cannot contain it.
secrets.on_compromise: Revoke; images are signed and pulled by digest, so a stolen pull token exposes source only.

secrets.name: ssh_deploy_key
secrets.description: Private key of the CI deploy identity (coordinator ruling b): production deploys run ONLY from CI, through the bastion's forward-only dfci account, to the dfdeploy account whose authorized_keys line carries the forced command df-deploy-ssh (only 'secrets-install' and 'deploy <digest>'). One per environment. UNTIL df-deploy verifies releases with cosign (round 2) this key is ROOT-EQUIVALENT IN EFFECT (it can drive df-secrets-install and df-deploy as root) and must be protected like root: GitHub environment secret with required reviewers, never on a workstation.
secrets.on_compromise: REVOKE ON EVERY HOST NOW: the key lives in root-owned /etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d files that Terraform does not update on running hosts, so edit them through the DigitalOcean console on the bastion and each host (or replace the hosts); there is no remote revocation tool until the round 2 df-deploy refresh-keys. Review auth logs and df-deploy invocations; P0 for production.

secrets.store_of_record: the hardware key itself (plus a registered spare held by the owner)
secrets.name: operator_security_keys
secrets.description: FIDO2 hardware security keys (sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com), one or two per person, enrolled as admin_users in Terraform: per-person accounts on the bastion and the hosts, no shared human account (coordinator ruling b; plan 12.7 individual identities and MFA). The private half never leaves the hardware key; only the PUBLIC keys are in Terraform variables. Each key is installed with verify-required (coordinator ruling c): a login needs the key's touch AND its PIN (generate with ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O verify-required). Break-glass access uses these accounts; their only sudo rights are df-secrets-install (also --audit) and df-deploy psql.
secrets.on_compromise: Remove that person's keys from the root-owned authorized_keys files on the bastion and every host through the DigitalOcean console (Terraform does not reach running hosts); review auth logs.
